    Attention & the Transformer, gently

    After this lesson you can explain, in plain language, what attention does, why "self-attention" lets a model use context, what multi-head means, and how a Transformer block is assembled — enough to read the rest of the course without fear.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~20 min Prerequisites: Tokens & embeddings Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    We now have a sequence of token embeddings and a way to train networks. But a plain stack of layers treats each token in isolation — and language is all about relationships. In "the trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big," the word "it" means the trophy, and you only know that by looking at the rest of the sentence. The mechanism that lets a model do this look-around is attention, and the architecture built around it is the Transformer. This lesson stays at the intuition level; you do not need the math to use it.

    The problem attention solves

    To produce a good representation of a token, the model should mix in information from the other tokens that are relevant to it — and ignore the ones that aren't. "It" needs to gather meaning from "trophy"; "big" needs to gather from "trophy" and "suitcase." Different tokens need different neighbors. Attention is a learnable, content-based way to decide, for each token, which other tokens to pull from and how much.

    Self-attention, in three moves

    For every token, the model derives three vectors from its embedding (each via learned weights):

    • a query — "what am I looking for?"
    • a key — "what do I offer to others?"
    • a value — "the information I'll hand over if chosen."

    Then, for a given token, the model compares its query against every token's key to get a relevance score, turns those scores into weights that sum to 1 (a softmax — the same operation we'll use for next-token probabilities), and takes the weighted average of all the values. The result replaces the token's representation with a blend of the information it found most relevant. Because every token attends to tokens in the same sequence, this is called self-attention.

    For readers who want the formula, the whole thing is one line: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V (Vaswani et al. 2017, arXiv 1706.03762). Q Kᵀ is every query dotted with every key (the relevance scores), dividing by √d (the square root of the vector width) keeps those scores from growing just because the vectors are long, and the softmax-weighted sum of V is the blend. You can skip the formula and keep the intuition; the Try it at the end of this lesson works one through with small numbers.

    Key idea

    Attention is a soft, learned lookup: each token asks a question (query), every token advertises (key), and the answer is a relevance-weighted mix of what they offer (values). Nothing is hand-wired — the query/key/value projections are parameters trained by gradient descent.

    Many heads, looking for different things

    One attention pattern can only capture one kind of relationship. Real language has many at once: subject–verb agreement, pronoun reference, adjective–noun, topic. So the model runs several attention computations in parallel — multi-head attention — each with its own query/key/value weights, free to specialize in a different pattern. Their outputs are combined. Heads aren't told what to specialize in; they differentiate during training.

    The Transformer block

    Attention is the centerpiece, but a Transformer block wraps it with a few supporting parts, and the model stacks many such blocks (SmolLM2-135M has 30, and the largest open models have 80 or more: small models are deep and narrow):

    • Multi-head self-attention — mix information across tokens (what we just covered).
    • A feed-forward network — a small neural net (from Lesson 0.3) applied to each token independently, to transform the mixed representation.
    • Residual connections — add each sub-layer's input to its output, so information and gradients flow cleanly through a deep stack.
    • Normalization — rescales activations to keep training stable.

    You don't need to memorize these. The thing to retain: a Transformer is a tall stack of blocks, each of which lets every token gather context (attention) and then think about it (feed-forward), with residuals and normalization keeping the whole tower trainable.

    The modern block: what changed since 2017

    The list above is the 2017 design. The roles are unchanged, but almost every open model you will fine-tune in 2026 (Llama, Qwen, SmolLM2, Mistral and their relatives) swaps in four refinements. You will meet their names in configs, in LoRA target lists and in memory math, so here they are once:

    • RMSNorm, applied before each sub-layer. The original LayerNorm subtracted the mean and divided by the spread; RMSNorm only divides by the root-mean-square, which is cheaper and works as well (Zhang & Sennrich 2019, arXiv 1910.07467). Placing the norm before attention and the feed-forward ("pre-norm") rather than after makes deep stacks easier to train (Xiong et al. 2020, arXiv 2002.04745).
    • A gated feed-forward network (SwiGLU). Instead of two matrices with an activation between them, there are three: a gate and an up projection widen each token's vector, the SiLU-activated gate multiplies the up projection element by element, and a down projection shrinks it back (Shazeer 2020, arXiv 2002.05202). In SmolLM2-135M the width goes 576 → 1,536 → 576.
    • Rotary positions (RoPE) inside attention. Word order enters by rotating each query and key by its position (Lesson 0.4), not by adding a position vector to the embeddings.
    • Grouped-query attention (GQA). Several query heads share one key head and one value head (Ainslie et al. 2023, arXiv 2305.13245). SmolLM2-135M has 9 query heads but only 3 key/value heads. The model gets nearly the same quality while storing a third of the keys and values, which matters for the KV cache below.

    Most of these models also drop the biases from their linear layers. You can see all of it by printing one block of the course model. This runs on a laptop CPU in seconds:

    import torch
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM

name = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M"
cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(name)
print(cfg.num_hidden_layers, cfg.hidden_size, cfg.num_attention_heads,
      cfg.num_key_value_heads, cfg.intermediate_size, cfg.hidden_act)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(name, dtype=torch.float32)  # a CPU is fine
print(model.model.layers[0])                       # one Transformer block
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))  # every parameter

    The first line prints 30 576 9 3 1536 silu. The block shows q_proj 576→576 but k_proj and v_proj only 576→192 (3 key/value heads of width 64: that is GQA), the three SwiGLU matrices gate_proj, up_proj and down_proj, two LlamaRMSNorm layers, and bias=False everywhere. The total is 134,515,008 parameters. These module names are exactly what LoRA's target_modules refers to in Track 1.

    Not every 2026 small model is a pure Transformer. Some hybrids replace most attention layers with cheaper linear-attention or state-space layers and keep only a few full-attention ones: Qwen3.5-2B has 18 linear-attention and 6 full-attention layers. Lesson 0.7 covers them.

    One detail that matters for generation: causal masking

    The language models in this course are decoder-only (also called causal). When predicting the next token, a token is only allowed to attend to tokens before it — never ahead. This causal mask is what makes "predict the next token" a fair game: the model can't peek at the answer it's supposed to produce. It's why the same trained network can both read a prompt and continue it, one token at a time.

    Why it scales, and what it costs

    Attention compares every token with every other token, so its work grows with the square of the sequence length: double the context and the attention work roughly quadruples. That sounds bad, but it is all independent multiplications a GPU can run at once, whereas a recurrent network (an LSTM, Lesson 0.6) has to read a sequence one step at a time. LSTMs can carry long-range context too, just more slowly to train and less reliably over long spans. Parallel training is the main reason Transformers took over.

    When generating, the model saves every earlier token's keys and values in a KV cache instead of recomputing them, so each new token costs work in proportion to the context so far. The cache costs memory: for SmolLM2-135M in bf16 it is 2 (K and V) × 30 layers × 3 KV heads × 64 × 2 bytes = 23,040 bytes per token, about 189 MB (180 MiB) for a full 8,192-token context. Without GQA's sharing (9 KV heads) it would be three times that. Serving and inference builds on this.

    Where we are

    We can now see the whole pipe: text → tokens → embeddings → a stack of Transformer blocks that contextualize each token. The only missing piece is how the model turns that final per-token representation into an actual next-token prediction — and how it generates text from there. That is Lesson 0.8, and it ties Track 0 together. First come two optional context lessons, Lessons 0.6 and 0.7: a brief history of language models and the three architecture families. Read them now or skip straight to Lesson 0.8.

    Recap

    • Attention lets each token blend in information from the tokens most relevant to it, using learned queries, keys and values; many heads track different relationships.
    • A Transformer stacks blocks of attention plus feed-forward, with residuals and normalization; today's blocks use RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE and grouped-query attention.
    • The causal mask lets each token see only the past, which makes next-token training fair; the KV cache makes generation cheaper at the price of memory.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Work one attention step by hand. A query q = [1, 0] meets three keys, k₁ = [2, 0], k₂ = [0, 2] and k₃ = [1, 1], whose values are the single numbers 10, 0 and 5. The width is d = 2. Compute the scores q·k / √2, the softmax weights, and the output.

    Show answer

    Dot products: 2, 0, 1. Divided by √2 ≈ 1.414: 1.414, 0, 0.707. Exponentials: 4.113, 1, 2.028, which sum to 7.141, so the weights are 0.576, 0.140, 0.284 (they sum to 1). Output: 0.576 × 10 + 0.140 × 0 + 0.284 × 5 ≈ 7.18. The query matched the first key best, so the first value dominates, but the others still contribute. Without the √2 the weights would be 0.665, 0.090, 0.245: sharper. With 64-wide heads the scaling matters far more.

    Key terms

    Attention
    A learned, content-based mechanism for a token to pull information from relevant tokens.
    Self-attention
    Attention where tokens attend to other tokens in the same sequence.
    Query / key / value
    Per-token vectors: what I seek, what I offer, what I hand over when chosen.
    Multi-head attention
    Several attention computations in parallel, each specializing in a different relationship.
    Scaled dot-product attention
    softmax(Q Kᵀ / √d) V: score every key against the query, normalise, blend the values.
    Transformer block
    Self-attention + feed-forward network + residual connections + normalization; stacked many times.
    RMSNorm / pre-norm
    The normalization most current models use, applied before each sub-layer rather than after.
    SwiGLU
    A gated feed-forward network with three matrices (gate, up, down) and a SiLU activation.
    Grouped-query attention (GQA)
    Several query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache with little quality loss.
    KV cache
    The stored keys and values of earlier tokens, so generation does not recompute them; it grows with context length.
    Causal mask (decoder-only)
    Restricting each token to attend only to earlier tokens, so next-token prediction is fair.
